extracted.intended_audience: writers, students of literature, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing, translating, and judging literature (fiction, style, criticism) focused on aesthetic beauty, truth, moral effect, erudition, and enduring value. Includes standards for faithful translation and balanced critical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of art: the beautiful
rubrics_metrics.description: “Fiction has no business to exist unless it is more beautiful than reality. ... in literature the one aim of art is the beautiful.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary works should seek beauty as their principal artistic end; anything grotesque or merely sensational that fails to achieve beauty does not properly belong to literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monstrosities/sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: “The monstrosities of fiction may be found in the booksellers' shops ... they have no place in literature.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that trade in transient shock or monstrosity (sold for a price and talked of for days) are not true literature; avoid producing or valuing sensationalism over aesthetic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erudition and knowledge (anti-ignorance)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Ignorance, which in matters of morals extenuates the crime, is itself, in matters of literature, a crime of the first order.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and critics must be well-informed; ignorance in literary matters is a serious failing. Learning and knowledge are necessary foundations for legitimate literary work and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope and modesty of talent
rubrics_metrics.description: “A small talent, if it keeps within its limits and rightly fulfils its task, may reach the goal just as well as a greater one.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should recognize and work within their natural range: modest, well-executed work that fulfils its proper function is preferable to overreaching that fails to do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate intellectual tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: “To accustom mankind to pleasures which depend neither upon the bodily appetites nor upon money, by giving them a taste for the things of the mind, seems to me ... the one proper fruit which nature has meant our literary productions to have.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literature's function is to foster non-material, intellectual pleasures and tastes; value works that elevate readers' capacity for enjoying the life of the mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating sects, crotchets, and divisiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: “Books which absorb our attention to such a degree that they rob us of all fancy for other books, are absolutely pernicious. ... they only bring fresh crotchets and sects into the world; they multiply ... measures; they are morally and politically a nuisance.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of works that monopolize attention and generate factionalism or doctrinal sects; literature should not encourage narrow, factional thinking or social/political nuisance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endurance depends on inherent truth (re-readability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The acceptableness of a work to future generations depends on its inherent truth; works that merely suit the taste of a generation are transitory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate literature by whether it contains a deep, illuminating truth that rewards repeated reading and persists beyond contemporary fashions; ephemeral pleasure alone does not secure permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth/Light vs. Pleasure: seek illumination
rubrics_metrics.description: “Truth illuminates and gives joy, and it is by the bond of joy, not of pleasure, that men's spirits are indissolubly held.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for writing that imparts light and joy (deep understanding and lasting satisfaction) rather than mere immediate pleasure; prefer works that enlighten rather than merely entertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balanced critical judgment (mind and soul)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism should be exercised with all the powers of the mind and soul at work together in due combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good criticism combines intellectual rigour with moral and emotional insight (example: Joubert's balanced judgments of Voltaire and Rousseau); avoid purely intellectual or purely rhetorical judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied and appropriate style
rubrics_metrics.description: Bossuet 'employs all our idioms' and turns 'the language of kings, of statesmen, and of warriors ... the trivial and the stately' into a style 'simple, grave, majestic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style should be adaptable to different registers and purposes; the best writers use a range of idioms and tones, combining common and sublime to suit subject and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate and philosophically informed translation
rubrics_metrics.description: A translator must render original texts faithfully and possess accurate knowledge of the source language (Latin) and sufficient philosophical familiarity; poor translation can spoil a work's reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translations should be both linguistically accurate and sensitive to philosophical meaning; when a translator lacks Latin accuracy, collaboration with a Latin expert is recommended to produce a reliable version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beneficial use of predecessors without dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: “Plato shows us nothing, but he brings brightness with him ... It is good to breathe his air, but not to live upon him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers should be influenced by great predecessors in ways that sharpen understanding and taste, but must avoid slavish dependence or living entirely off another's ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional truth and moral effect of fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may create novels that 'harrow our hearts,' but the soul may respond 'You hurt me.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiction should handle suffering and passion with moral sensitivity; avoid gratuitous emotional harm or manipulation that displeases the reader's deeper moral sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity and union of soul with intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: The best literary quality is the union of soul with intellect; truths must be 'steeped in the soul' rather than merely intellectual epigrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value writing that stems from sincere moral feeling and lived conviction, not cleverness alone; the author's integrity and inner life should inform the work's truth and charm.
